To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mean-square displacments and self-diffusivites of particles in shear flow depend on the initial orientation of the particle, and that the mean-square displacement of a particle is a function of time and the shear rate.

the self-diffusivites of non-Brownain particles in shear flow are finite and often large, and the self-diffusion tensor is anisotropic and non-symmetric, with the largest diffusivities along the streamwise and spanwise directions.

the shear-induced self-difffusivity of a suspension of non-colloidal particles is anisotropic in the shear plane, the self-difffusive fluxes are not in general parallel to the mean velocity, and the diffusivity in the vorticity direction is not a constant, as has been assumed in the literature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the dynamics and structure of complex fluids, in particular, colloidal dispersions, suspensions, and emulsions.
the rheological behaviour of concentrated suspensions of non-colloidal particles.
the study of the self-diffusional motion of particles in non-colloids, which is a problem of great practical interest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self-diffusivites are isotropic and independent of the shear rate.

the mean-square displacement of a tracer particle in simple shear flow can be described in terms of a Fokker-Planck equation with a diffusivity tensor that depends on the shear rate and the particle volume fraction.

the shear-induced diffusivities are not simply related to the mean-square displactions, and the Fokker–Plank equation with a diffusion coefficient is not a correct description of the dynamics of the system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the monodisperse suspensions, the shear-induced diffusion is a linear process and the self-diffusivies are given by a simple linear combination of the diffusivities in a quiescent system and the shear-induced diffusivities in an infinite system.
the shear-induced self-difference in non-Brownian suspensions is a very slow process.

, for non-colloidal particles, the shear-induced self-dif-fusivities are well described by a Fokker-Planck equation with the diffusivities given by the usual Einstein relation, but the advection terms are not negligible.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while shear flow can induce a large enhancement of self-diffusional motion in the direction of the shear gradient, the diffusivity in the vorticity direction is always reduced.
the shear-induced self-difference tensor is anisotropic, even in monodisperse suspensions.
the self-diffusivites are very sensitive to the strain sampled by the experiment and the finite strain sampling can be used to extract the self-diffusion coefficient in a shear flow.
